```{=html}
<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix C <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Examples</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">C.5</span> Examples of Connections, Torsion and Curvature (§§<a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/connections-affine-manifolds.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Connections_Affine_Manifolds">6.1</a>–<a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/torsion-curvature.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Torsion_Curvature">6.4</a>)</h1></header>
<p>This appendix continues the example of Appendix <a class="dg-xref" href="example-fields.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Example_Fields">C.4</a>: same manifold, same two charts, same curves, fields and scalar field. On top of it we now place <em>three</em> different connections, chosen so that between them they display every notion of Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a>:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p><span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span>, flat and torsion free, whose autoparallels are straight lines in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span>;</p></li>
<li><p><span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)</span>, flat but with torsion, whose autoparallels include the circles <span class="math inline">\(\delta_{r_0}\)</span>;</p></li>
<li><p><span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\kappa}\)</span>, torsion free but curved, whose autoparallels are sinusoids and whose parallel transport around closed loops does not return vectors to themselves.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>A connection is additional structure: nothing in <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty})_2\)</span> singles one out, and in particular the egg-carton shape of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span> inside <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^3\)</span> plays no role in what follows. Only once a metric is introduced will a preferred connection appear. As in the rest of the notes, the Einstein summation convention is implied, and the connection coefficient functions follow the convention of Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a>, <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^i_{jk} \coloneqq dx^i\left\lceil \nabla_{\partial x_k} \partial x_j \right\rfloor\)</span>, whose <em>last</em> lower index labels the direction of differentiation.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">C.5.1</span> Setting`{=html} {#subsection_Example_Connections_setting}

```{=html}
<p>We write functions on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span> through the chart coordinates of their argument, <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}(p) = (a, b)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}(p) = (\beta_1, \beta_2)\)</span>, related on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{V}\)</span> by <span class="math display">\[
    a = \beta_1 \cos \beta_2, \qquad b = \beta_1 \sin \beta_2, \qquad \beta_1 = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} :
\]</span> expressions in <span class="math inline">\(a, b\)</span> refer to the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span>, and expressions in <span class="math inline">\(\beta_1, \beta_2\)</span> to the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span>. From Appendix <a class="dg-xref" href="example-fields.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Example_Fields">C.4</a> we only need the following objects.</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p><strong>The Jacobians</strong> of the transition maps (Subsection <a class="dg-xref" href="example-fields.html#subsection_Example_Fields_jacobians" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Example_Fields_jacobians">C.4.2</a>),  <span class="math display">\[
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} =
            \begin{bmatrix}
                \cos \beta_2 &amp; -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \\
                \sin \beta_2 &amp; \beta_1 \cos \beta_2
            \end{bmatrix}^s_{j},
            \qquad
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} =
            \begin{bmatrix}
                \cos \beta_2 &amp; \sin \beta_2 \\
                -\dfrac{\sin \beta_2}{\beta_1} &amp; \dfrac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1}
            \end{bmatrix}^i_{l},
        \]</span>  and hence the relations between the chart-induced basis fields on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} = \mathcal{V}\)</span>:  <span class="math display">\[
            \partial y_1 = \cos \beta_2 \, \partial x_1 + \sin \beta_2 \, \partial x_2 ,
            \qquad
            \partial y_2 = -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \, \partial x_1 + \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \, \partial x_2 .
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p><strong>The curves</strong> <span class="math inline">\(\gamma_{x_0}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\delta_{r_0}\)</span> (Subsection <a class="dg-xref" href="example-fields.html#subsection_Example_Fields_curves" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Example_Fields_curves">C.4.3</a>), through their chart representatives, from which their velocity and acceleration components follow by differentiation:  <span class="math display">\[
            \begin{array}{c@{\qquad}|@{\qquad}c}
                (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{x_0})(\lambda) = (x_0, \, \lambda) &amp;
                (\mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma_{x_0})(\lambda) = \left( \sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2}, \, \operatorname{atan2}(\lambda, x_0) \right) \\[8pt]
                (\mathscr{X} \circ \delta_{r_0})(\lambda) = (r_0 \cos \lambda, \, r_0 \sin \lambda) &amp;
                (\mathscr{Y} \circ \delta_{r_0})(\lambda) = (r_0, \, \lambda), \quad \lambda \in (-\pi, \pi)
            \end{array}
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p><strong>The vector fields</strong> <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y}\)</span> (Subsection <a class="dg-xref" href="example-fields.html#subsection_Example_Fields_vector_fields" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Example_Fields_vector_fields">C.4.5</a>), the velocity fields of the two families, whose component functions, in the notation of Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../fields/tensor-fields-and-notation.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Tensor_Fields_and_notation">5.3</a>, are  <span class="math display">\[
            \begin{array}{c@{\qquad}|@{\qquad}c}
                \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = x^i \, \partial x_i = \partial x_2 &amp;
                \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{V} = y^i \, \partial y_i = \sin \beta_2 \, \partial y_1 + \dfrac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2 \\[12pt]
                \left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \tilde{x}^i \, \partial x_i = -b \, \partial x_1 + a \, \partial x_2 &amp;
                \left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{V} = \tilde{y}^i \, \partial y_i = \partial y_2
            \end{array}
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p><strong>The scalar field</strong> <span class="math inline">\(f(p) = \cos a \cos b + 1\)</span> and its differential (Subsection <a class="dg-xref" href="example-fields.html#subsection_Example_Fields_function" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Example_Fields_function">C.4.4</a>), with component functions in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span>  <span class="math display">\[
            \left. df \right|_\mathcal{U} = \mathtt{x}_i \, dx^i, \qquad
            \mathtt{x}_1 = -\sin a \cos b, \qquad \mathtt{x}_2 = -\cos a \sin b .
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p><strong>The second derivatives of the chart transition</strong>, needed below. By Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a> they are the functions <span class="math inline">\(\frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \partial \mathscr{Y}^j}(p) = \partial_k \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^s \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right]\big( \mathscr{Y}(p) \big)\)</span>, i.e. the second partial derivatives of <span class="math inline">\((\beta_1, \beta_2) \mapsto (\beta_1 \cos \beta_2, \beta_1 \sin \beta_2)\)</span>:  <span class="math display">\[
            \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^1}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \partial \mathscr{Y}^j} =
            \begin{bmatrix}
                0 &amp; -\sin \beta_2 \\
                -\sin \beta_2 &amp; -\beta_1 \cos \beta_2
            \end{bmatrix}_{kj},
            \qquad
            \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^2}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \partial \mathscr{Y}^j} =
            \begin{bmatrix}
                0 &amp; \cos \beta_2 \\
                \cos \beta_2 &amp; -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2
            \end{bmatrix}_{kj}.
        \]</span></p></li>
</ul>
<p>Finally, recall how a connection is <em>specified</em> in practice. By Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a>, on a chart domain the whole action of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span> is fixed by the <span class="math inline">\(\dim(\mathcal{M})^3 = 8\)</span> connection coefficient functions: for any two vector fields, <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_\mathcal{Z} \mathcal{W} = \big( \mathcal{Z}\left\lfloor w^k \right\rceil + \Gamma^k_{ji} \, w^j z^i \big) \partial x_k\)</span>. Conversely, any choice of <span class="math inline">\(8\)</span> smooth functions on a chart domain defines, through this formula and the Leibniz rule, a connection there. Since <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U} = \mathcal{M}\)</span>, choosing the <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>’s in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> defines a connection on the whole manifold, and its coefficients in <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span> then follow from the transformation law.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">C.5.2</span> A flat, torsion-free connection: <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span>`{=html} {#subsection_Example_Connections_flat}

```{=html}
<p>Define <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span> on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span> by declaring all its connection coefficient functions in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> to vanish, <span class="math display">\[
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_x \right)^i_{jk} = 0, \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad \nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_{\partial x_k} \partial x_j = 0 ,
\]</span> the analogue on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span> of the familiar derivative of vector fields in the Euclidean plane, hence the label.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Coefficients in the polar chart.</strong> With <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_x = 0\)</span>, only the inhomogeneous term of the transformation law survives, <span class="math display">\[
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y \right)^i_{jk}
    = \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^s} \, \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \, \partial \mathscr{Y}^j}
    = \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \, \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^1}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \, \partial \mathscr{Y}^j}
    + \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^2} \, \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^2}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \, \partial \mathscr{Y}^j},
\]</span> which is symmetric in <span class="math inline">\(j\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(k\)</span>, leaving six independent entries. Taking the rows of <span class="math inline">\(\partial \mathscr{Y}^i / \partial \mathscr{X}^l\)</span> and the second derivatives listed above: <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y \right)^1_{11} &amp;= \cos \beta_2 \cdot 0 + \sin \beta_2 \cdot 0 = 0, \\
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y \right)^1_{12} = \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y \right)^1_{21}
    &amp;= \cos \beta_2 \, (-\sin \beta_2) + \sin \beta_2 \, \cos \beta_2 = 0, \\
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y \right)^1_{22}
    &amp;= \cos \beta_2 \, (-\beta_1 \cos \beta_2) + \sin \beta_2 \, (-\beta_1 \sin \beta_2) = -\beta_1, \\
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y \right)^2_{11} &amp;= -\frac{\sin \beta_2}{\beta_1} \cdot 0 + \frac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} \cdot 0 = 0, \\
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y \right)^2_{12} = \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y \right)^2_{21}
    &amp;= -\frac{\sin \beta_2}{\beta_1} \, (-\sin \beta_2) + \frac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} \, \cos \beta_2 = \frac{1}{\beta_1}, \\
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y \right)^2_{22}
    &amp;= -\frac{\sin \beta_2}{\beta_1} \, (-\beta_1 \cos \beta_2) + \frac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} \, (-\beta_1 \sin \beta_2) = 0 .
\end{align*}</span> The same connection thus has vanishing coefficients in one chart and non-vanishing ones in the other: the <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>’s are not the components of a tensor field. In terms of the basis fields, <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_{\partial y_2} \partial y_2 = -\beta_1 \, \partial y_1\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_{\partial y_1} \partial y_2 = \nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_{\partial y_2} \partial y_1 = \frac{1}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2\)</span>, while <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_{\partial y_1} \partial y_1 = 0\)</span>.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Torsion and curvature.</strong> In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> all <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>’s vanish, so <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}^i_{jk} = \Gamma^i_{kj} - \Gamma^i_{jk} = 0\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}^i_{jkm} = \partial x_k\left\lfloor \Gamma^i_{jm} \right\rceil - \partial x_m\left\lfloor \Gamma^i_{jk} \right\rceil + \Gamma^i_{rk} \Gamma^r_{jm} - \Gamma^i_{rm} \Gamma^r_{jk} = 0\)</span>. Both are tensor fields, so they vanish in every chart: <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span> is flat and torsion free. It is instructive to see this happen in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span>, where the <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>’s do not vanish. Torsion freeness is the symmetry <span class="math inline">\((\Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y)^2_{12} = (\Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y)^2_{21}\)</span>. As for the curvature, in two dimensions and thanks to the antisymmetry in the last two indices, the independent components are <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}^i_{j12}\)</span>, and, with <span class="math inline">\(\partial y_k\)</span> acting on functions as <span class="math inline">\(\partial / \partial \beta_k\)</span>, <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{Riem}^1_{212}
    &amp;= \partial y_1\left\lfloor \Gamma^1_{22} \right\rceil - \partial y_2\left\lfloor \Gamma^1_{21} \right\rceil
    + \Gamma^1_{r1} \Gamma^r_{22} - \Gamma^1_{r2} \Gamma^r_{21}
    = -1 - 0 + 0 - \Gamma^1_{22} \Gamma^2_{21}
    = -1 + \beta_1 \cdot \frac{1}{\beta_1} = 0, \\
    \mathrm{Riem}^2_{112}
    &amp;= \partial y_1\left\lfloor \Gamma^2_{12} \right\rceil - \partial y_2\left\lfloor \Gamma^2_{11} \right\rceil
    + \Gamma^2_{r1} \Gamma^r_{12} - \Gamma^2_{r2} \Gamma^r_{11}
    = -\frac{1}{\beta_1^2} - 0 + \Gamma^2_{21} \Gamma^2_{12} - 0
    = -\frac{1}{\beta_1^2} + \frac{1}{\beta_1^2} = 0,
\end{align*}</span> while <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}^1_{112}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}^2_{212}\)</span> vanish term by term. The derivatives of the <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>’s and their quadratic terms cancel exactly, as they must. ✓</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Covariant derivatives of the example fields.</strong> In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> the covariant derivative reduces to the action of the vector field on the component functions. Hence <span class="math display">\[
    \nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{Y}\left\lfloor x^k \right\rceil \partial x_k = 0,
    \qquad
    \nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor \tilde{x}^k \right\rceil \partial x_k
    = \partial x_2\left\lfloor -b \right\rceil \partial x_1 + \partial x_2\left\lfloor a \right\rceil \partial x_2 = -\partial x_1 ,
\]</span> since the components of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}\)</span> are constant. The same results must come out of the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span>, where the components are <em>not</em> constant and the <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>’s compensate for it. With <span class="math inline">\((\nabla_\mathcal{Z} \mathcal{W})^k = \mathcal{Z}\left\lfloor w^k \right\rceil + \Gamma^k_{ji} \, w^j z^i\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\tilde{y}^i = (0,1)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(y^i = (\sin \beta_2, \cos \beta_2 / \beta_1)\)</span>: <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \left( \nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} \right)^1
    &amp;= \partial y_2\left\lfloor \sin \beta_2 \right\rceil + \Gamma^1_{22} \, y^2
    = \cos \beta_2 - \beta_1 \, \frac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} = 0, \\
    \left( \nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} \right)^2
    &amp;= \partial y_2\left\lfloor \frac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} \right\rceil + \Gamma^2_{12} \, y^1
    = -\frac{\sin \beta_2}{\beta_1} + \frac{\sin \beta_2}{\beta_1} = 0, \quad \checkmark
\end{align*}</span> and, since the components of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y}\)</span> are constant in <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span>, <span class="math display">\[
    \nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} = \Gamma^k_{2i} \, y^i \, \partial y_k
    = \Gamma^1_{22} \, y^2 \, \partial y_1 + \Gamma^2_{21} \, y^1 \, \partial y_2
    = -\cos \beta_2 \, \partial y_1 + \frac{\sin \beta_2}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2 ,
\]</span> which, using the relations between the basis fields, is <span class="math inline">\(-\cos \beta_2 (\cos \beta_2 \, \partial x_1 + \sin \beta_2 \, \partial x_2) + \sin \beta_2 (-\sin \beta_2 \, \partial x_1 + \cos \beta_2 \, \partial x_2) = -\partial x_1\)</span>. ✓ Torsion freeness can also be checked on these two fields: their commutator is <span class="math inline">\([\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}] = [\partial x_2, -b \, \partial x_1 + a \, \partial x_2] = \partial x_2\left\lfloor -b \right\rceil \partial x_1 + \partial x_2\left\lfloor a \right\rceil \partial x_2 = -\partial x_1\)</span>, so that <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} - \nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} - [\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}] = -\partial x_1 - 0 + \partial x_1 = 0\)</span>. ✓</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>For the covector field <span class="math inline">\(df\)</span>, the formula <span class="math inline">\((\nabla_\mathcal{Z} df)_k = \mathcal{Z}\left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_k \right\rceil - \Gamma^j_{ki} \, \mathtt{x}_j \, z^i\)</span> gives, in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span>, <span class="math display">\[
    \nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} df = \partial x_2\left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_k \right\rceil dx^k
    = \sin a \sin b \; dx^1 - \cos a \cos b \; dx^2 ,
\]</span> i.e. the components of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}} df\)</span> are the ordinary second partial derivatives of <span class="math inline">\(f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\)</span>, as expected for a connection whose coefficients vanish in that chart.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Autoparallels.</strong> The autoparallel equation <span class="math inline">\(\ddot{\gamma}^k + \Gamma^k_{ji}(\gamma(\lambda)) \, \dot{\gamma}^i \dot{\gamma}^j = 0\)</span> reads, in each chart, <span class="math display">\[
    \begin{array}{c@{\qquad}|@{\qquad}c}
        \text{chart } \mathscr{X}: &amp;
        \text{chart } \mathscr{Y}: \\[4pt]
        \begin{cases}
            \ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{U} = 0 \\
            \ddot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = 0
        \end{cases}
        &amp;
        \begin{cases}
            \ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{V} - \gamma^1_\mathcal{V} \, \big( \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} \big)^2 = 0 \\[4pt]
            \ddot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} + \dfrac{2}{\gamma^1_\mathcal{V}} \, \dot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{V} \, \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} = 0
        \end{cases}
    \end{array}
\]</span> where <span class="math inline">\(\gamma^1_\mathcal{V} \coloneqq \mathscr{Y}^1 \circ \gamma\)</span> is the radial chart coordinate along the curve, and in the second equation both <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^2_{12}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^2_{21}\)</span> contribute. In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> the solutions are <span class="math inline">\((\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma)(\lambda) = (a_0, b_0) + \lambda \, (u, v)\)</span>: <strong>the autoparallels of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span> are the curves whose chart representatives in <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> are straight lines</strong>, traversed at constant speed. In particular:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p><span class="math inline">\(\gamma_{x_0}\)</span> is autoparallel, since <span class="math inline">\((\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{x_0})(\lambda) = (x_0, \lambda)\)</span>. In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span> its representative is curved, yet it solves the corresponding equations: differentiating it,  <span class="math display">\[
            \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{V} = \left( \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2}}, \, \frac{x_0}{x_0^2 + \lambda^2} \right),
            \qquad
            \ddot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{V} = \left( \frac{x_0^2}{(x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^{3/2}}, \, -\frac{2 x_0 \lambda}{(x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^2} \right),
        \]</span>  so that  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            &amp;\frac{x_0^2}{(x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^{3/2}} - \sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2} \, \frac{x_0^2}{(x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^2} = 0, \\
            &amp;-\frac{2 x_0 \lambda}{(x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^2} + \frac{2}{\sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2}} \, \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2}} \, \frac{x_0}{x_0^2 + \lambda^2} = 0. \quad \checkmark
        \end{align*}</span>  At field level, this is the statement <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor x^k \right\rceil \partial x_k = 0\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><span class="math inline">\(\delta_{r_0}\)</span> is <em>not</em> autoparallel. Its acceleration, computed in either chart,  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \text{chart } \mathscr{X}: \quad a_{\delta}(\lambda) &amp;= \ddot{\delta}^k_\mathcal{U} \, \partial x_k = -r_0 \cos \lambda \, \partial x_1 - r_0 \sin \lambda \, \partial x_2, \\
            \text{chart } \mathscr{Y}: \quad a_{\delta}(\lambda) &amp;= \big( 0 + \Gamma^1_{22} \cdot 1 \big) \partial y_1 + \big( 0 + 2 \, \Gamma^2_{12} \cdot 0 \cdot 1 \big) \partial y_2 = -r_0 \, \partial y_1 ,
        \end{align*}</span>  is the same vector (use <span class="math inline">\(\partial y_1 = \cos \lambda \, \partial x_1 + \sin \lambda \, \partial x_2\)</span> along the curve), pointing towards the origin. Since it is not proportional to the velocity <span class="math inline">\(\partial y_2\)</span>, not even a reparametrization of <span class="math inline">\(\delta_{r_0}\)</span> is autoparallel. At field level, <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{Y} = -\beta_1 \, \partial y_1 \neq 0\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Parallel transport.</strong> Let <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Z}\)</span> be a vector field along a curve <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span> with components <span class="math inline">\(z^k(\lambda)\)</span> in a chart. By the same argument used for the autoparallel equation, <span class="math inline">\((\nabla_{v_{\gamma(\lambda)}} \mathcal{Z})^k = \dot{z}^k + \Gamma^k_{ji}(\gamma(\lambda)) \, z^j \, \dot{\gamma}^i\)</span>, so parallel transport along <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span> is the linear system of ODEs <span class="math display">\[
    \dot{z}^k(\lambda) + \Gamma^k_{ji}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, z^j(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^i(\lambda) = 0 .
\]</span> For <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span> in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> this is <span class="math inline">\(\dot{z}^k = 0\)</span>: <strong>parallel transport keeps the cartesian components constant</strong>, along any curve. Hence <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}\)</span> is parallel along every curve, whereas <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y}\)</span> is parallel along none of our curves, e.g. <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} = -\partial x_1 \neq 0\)</span> along <span class="math inline">\(\gamma_{x_0}\)</span>. Transporting an initial vector with cartesian components <span class="math inline">\((c_1, c_2)\)</span> along <span class="math inline">\(\delta_{r_0}\)</span>, where <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\delta}^i_\mathcal{V} = (0,1)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\beta_1 = r_0\)</span>, the polar components must instead solve <span class="math display">\[
    \dot{z}^1 + \Gamma^1_{22} \, z^2 = \dot{z}^1 - r_0 \, z^2 = 0,
    \qquad
    \dot{z}^2 + \Gamma^2_{12} \, z^1 = \dot{z}^2 + \frac{1}{r_0} \, z^1 = 0,
\]</span> whose solution is <span class="math inline">\(z^1(\lambda) = c_1 \cos \lambda + c_2 \sin \lambda\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(z^2(\lambda) = (-c_1 \sin \lambda + c_2 \cos \lambda) / r_0\)</span>. Converting back with <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\)</span> gives <span class="math inline">\(\cos \lambda \, z^1 - r_0 \sin \lambda \, z^2 = c_1\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\sin \lambda \, z^1 + r_0 \cos \lambda \, z^2 = c_2\)</span>. ✓ The transported vector keeps its cartesian direction while its polar components rotate. After a full turn it returns to itself, as it must for a flat connection.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">C.5.3</span> A flat connection with torsion: <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)</span>`{=html} {#subsection_Example_Connections_torsion}

```{=html}
<p>The second connection is built by declaring a frame, rather than a chart, to be parallel. On <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}^* \coloneqq \mathcal{M} \setminus \{ (0, 0, h(0,0)) \}\)</span>, i.e. where <span class="math inline">\(a^2 + b^2 &gt; 0\)</span>, consider the unit radial and angular vector fields <span class="math display">\[
    e_1 \coloneqq \frac{a \, \partial x_1 + b \, \partial x_2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}},
    \qquad
    e_2 \coloneqq \frac{-b \, \partial x_1 + a \, \partial x_2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}},
\]</span> which on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{V}\)</span> read <span class="math inline">\(e_1 = \partial y_1\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(e_2 = \frac{1}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2\)</span>. They form a frame at every point of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}^*\)</span>, but, unlike <span class="math inline">\(\{ \partial x_i \}\)</span> or <span class="math inline">\(\{ \partial y_i \}\)</span>, not a chart-induced one. Define <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)</span> by <span class="math display">\[
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Z} \, e_a = 0 \qquad \forall \, \mathcal{Z} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}^*, \; a = 1, 2 .
\]</span> By the product rule this fixes the connection completely: any vector field is <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{W} = w^a e_a\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(w^a \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M}^*)\)</span>, and then <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Z} \mathcal{W} = \mathcal{Z}\left\lfloor w^a \right\rceil e_a\)</span>. A connection of this kind, which makes a global frame parallel, is called a <strong>teleparallel</strong> (or Weitzenböck) connection, hence the label.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Coefficients in the polar chart.</strong> Since <span class="math inline">\(\partial y_1 = e_1\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\partial y_2 = \beta_1 \, e_2\)</span>, the product rule gives <span class="math display">\[
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial y_k} \partial y_1 = 0,
    \qquad
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial y_k} \partial y_2 = \partial y_k\left\lfloor \mathscr{Y}^1 \right\rceil e_2 = \delta^1_k \, e_2 = \frac{\delta^1_k}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2 ,
\]</span> so that the only non-vanishing coefficient function is <span class="math display">\[
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_y \right)^2_{21} = \frac{1}{\beta_1}
    \qquad \big( \text{while } \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_y \right)^2_{12} = 0 \big).
\]</span></p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Coefficients in the cartesian chart.</strong> Inverting the definition of the frame, <span class="math display">\[
    \partial x_1 = \frac{a \, e_1 - b \, e_2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}},
    \qquad
    \partial x_2 = \frac{b \, e_1 + a \, e_2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}},
\]</span> and the product rule, with the frame fields parallel, gives <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_k} \partial x_1
    &amp;= \partial x_k\left\lfloor \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \right\rceil e_1 - \partial x_k\left\lfloor \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \right\rceil e_2, \\
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_k} \partial x_2
    &amp;= \partial x_k\left\lfloor \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \right\rceil e_1 + \partial x_k\left\lfloor \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \right\rceil e_2 .
\end{align*}</span> The four derivatives needed are <span class="math display">\begin{gather*}
    \partial x_1\left\lfloor \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \right\rceil = \frac{b^2}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}}, \qquad
    \partial x_2\left\lfloor \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \right\rceil = \frac{a^2}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}}, \\
    \partial x_2\left\lfloor \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \right\rceil = \partial x_1\left\lfloor \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \right\rceil = -\frac{a b}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}},
\end{gather*}</span> and, re-expressing <span class="math inline">\(b \, e_1 + a \, e_2 = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \; \partial x_2\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(a \, e_1 - b \, e_2 = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \; \partial x_1\)</span>, <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_1} \partial x_1 &amp;= \frac{b \, \big( b \, e_1 + a \, e_2 \big)}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{b}{a^2 + b^2} \, \partial x_2,
    &amp;
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_2} \partial x_1 &amp;= -\frac{a \, \big( b \, e_1 + a \, e_2 \big)}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}} = -\frac{a}{a^2 + b^2} \, \partial x_2, \\
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_1} \partial x_2 &amp;= -\frac{b \, \big( a \, e_1 - b \, e_2 \big)}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}} = -\frac{b}{a^2 + b^2} \, \partial x_1,
    &amp;
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_2} \partial x_2 &amp;= \frac{a \, \big( a \, e_1 - b \, e_2 \big)}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{a}{a^2 + b^2} \, \partial x_1,
\end{align*}</span> i.e. the non-vanishing coefficient functions in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> are <span class="math display">\[
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x \right)^2_{11} = \frac{b}{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x \right)^2_{12} = -\frac{a}{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x \right)^1_{21} = -\frac{b}{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad
    \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x \right)^1_{22} = \frac{a}{a^2 + b^2} .
\]</span></p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>The two connections differ by a tensor field.</strong> Although neither set of <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>’s is tensorial, their difference is: the inhomogeneous terms, which depend only on the charts, cancel in the transformation law. In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span>, the difference <span class="math inline">\(D \coloneqq \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}} - \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span> has components <span class="math display">\[
    D^1_{22} = 0 - (-\beta_1) = \beta_1, \qquad D^2_{12} = 0 - \frac{1}{\beta_1} = -\frac{1}{\beta_1}, \qquad D^2_{21} = \frac{1}{\beta_1} - \frac{1}{\beta_1} = 0,
\]</span> and, since <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_x = 0\)</span>, its components in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> must be exactly <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x\)</span>. Checking one of them with the <span class="math inline">\((1,2)\)</span>-tensor transformation law, <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    D^1_{22}\big|_\mathscr{X}
    &amp;= \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^1}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^l} \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^s}{\partial \mathscr{X}^2} \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^p}{\partial \mathscr{X}^2} \, D^l_{sp}
    = \cos \beta_2 \left( \frac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} \right)^2 \beta_1
    + \left( -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \right) \sin \beta_2 \, \frac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} \left( -\frac{1}{\beta_1} \right) \\
    &amp;= \frac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1},
\end{align*}</span> which is indeed <span class="math inline">\(\left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x \right)^1_{22} = a / (a^2 + b^2)\)</span> written in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span>, since <span class="math inline">\(a = \beta_1 \cos \beta_2\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(a^2 + b^2 = \beta_1^2\)</span>. ✓Note also that <span class="math inline">\(D^i_{j1} = 0\)</span>: the two connections agree when differentiating along <span class="math inline">\(\partial y_1\)</span>, i.e. radially, and differ only in the angular direction.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Torsion.</strong> In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}^2_{12} = \Gamma^2_{21} - \Gamma^2_{12} = \frac{1}{\beta_1} = -\mathtt{T}^2_{21}\)</span>, all other components vanishing, i.e. <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}(\cdot, \partial y_1, \partial y_2) = \frac{1}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2\)</span>. In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span>, <span class="math display">\[
    \mathtt{T}^1_{12} = \Gamma^1_{21} - \Gamma^1_{12} = -\frac{b}{a^2 + b^2},
    \qquad
    \mathtt{T}^2_{12} = \Gamma^2_{21} - \Gamma^2_{12} = \frac{a}{a^2 + b^2},
\]</span> i.e. <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}(\cdot, \partial x_1, \partial x_2) = \big( -b \, \partial x_1 + a \, \partial x_2 \big) / (a^2 + b^2) = \mathcal{Y} / (a^2 + b^2)\)</span>. Both results describe the same tensor field: since <span class="math inline">\(\partial y_j = \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, \partial x_s\)</span>, bilinearity and antisymmetry give <span class="math display">\[
    \mathtt{T}(\cdot, \partial y_1, \partial y_2)
    = \det\!\left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right) \mathtt{T}(\cdot, \partial x_1, \partial x_2)
    = \beta_1 \cdot \frac{1}{\beta_1^2} \, \partial y_2 = \frac{1}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2 ,
\]</span> using <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y} = \partial y_2\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(a^2 + b^2 = \beta_1^2\)</span>. ✓ The origin of the torsion is transparent in the frame: since <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}} e_a = 0\)</span>, <span class="math display">\[
    \mathtt{T}(\cdot, e_1, e_2) = -[e_1, e_2] = -\Big[ \partial y_1, \frac{1}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2 \Big]
    = -\partial y_1\left\lfloor \frac{1}{\mathscr{Y}^1} \right\rceil \partial y_2 = \frac{1}{\beta_1^2} \, \partial y_2 = \frac{1}{\beta_1} \, e_2 :
\]</span> <strong>a connection that declares a non-chart-induced frame parallel has a torsion measuring how much the frame fields fail to commute</strong>. As a last check, take our two fields in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span>, where, in terms of the frame, <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X} = \sin \beta_2 \, \partial y_1 + \frac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2 = \sin \beta_2 \, e_1 + \cos \beta_2 \, e_2\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y} = \partial y_2 = \beta_1 \, e_2\)</span>. Since the frame is parallel, only the frame components get differentiated: <span class="math display">\[
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor \mathscr{Y}^1 \right\rceil e_2 = \sin \beta_2 \, e_2,
    \qquad
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} = \partial y_2\left\lfloor \sin \beta_2 \right\rceil e_1 + \partial y_2\left\lfloor \cos \beta_2 \right\rceil e_2
    = \cos \beta_2 \, e_1 - \sin \beta_2 \, e_2 ,
\]</span> where <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}\left\lfloor \mathscr{Y}^1 \right\rceil = y^1 = \sin \beta_2\)</span>. Their commutator, <span class="math inline">\([\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}] = -\partial x_1 = -\cos \beta_2 \, \partial y_1 + \frac{\sin \beta_2}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2 = -\cos \beta_2 \, e_1 + \sin \beta_2 \, e_2\)</span>, was computed in Subsection <a class="dg-xref" href="#subsection_Example_Connections_flat" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Example_Connections_flat">C.5.2</a>, so that <span class="math display">\[
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} - \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} - [\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}]
    = \sin \beta_2 \, e_2 - \cos \beta_2 \, e_1 + \sin \beta_2 \, e_2 + \cos \beta_2 \, e_1 - \sin \beta_2 \, e_2
    = \sin \beta_2 \, e_2 ,
\]</span> in agreement with <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}(\cdot, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = y^1 \, \mathtt{T}(\cdot, \partial y_1, \partial y_2) = \sin \beta_2 \, \frac{1}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2 = \sin \beta_2 \, e_2\)</span>, the term with <span class="math inline">\(y^2\)</span> dropping out by antisymmetry. ✓</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Curvature.</strong> Since the frame is parallel, <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Y} e_a - \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Y} \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} e_a - \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_{[\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}]} e_a = 0\)</span> for <span class="math inline">\(a = 1, 2\)</span>, and by <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty(\mathcal{M}^*)\)</span>-linearity in the slot of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Z}\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem} = 0\)</span>: <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)</span> is flat. In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span> this is immediate: every term of <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}^i_{j12} = \partial y_1\left\lfloor \Gamma^i_{j2} \right\rceil - \partial y_2\left\lfloor \Gamma^i_{j1} \right\rceil + \Gamma^i_{r1} \Gamma^r_{j2} - \Gamma^i_{r2} \Gamma^r_{j1}\)</span> contains either a coefficient with last index <span class="math inline">\(2\)</span>, all of which vanish, or the derivative <span class="math inline">\(\partial y_2\left\lfloor \Gamma^i_{j1} \right\rceil\)</span>, which vanishes since <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^2_{21} = 1/\beta_1\)</span> does not depend on <span class="math inline">\(\beta_2\)</span>. <strong>Curvature and torsion are thus independent notions</strong>: <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)</span> are both flat, and only the latter has torsion.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>A covariant derivative compared.</strong> For the same scalar field <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> and direction <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X} = \partial x_2\)</span>, the two connections give different covariant derivatives of <span class="math inline">\(df\)</span>. In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(x^i = (0,1)\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\((\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} df)_k = \partial x_2\left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_k \right\rceil - \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x \right)^j_{k2} \mathtt{x}_j\)</span>, so that <span class="math display">\[
    \nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} df
    = \left( \sin a \sin b - \frac{a \cos a \sin b}{a^2 + b^2} \right) dx^1
    + \left( -\cos a \cos b + \frac{a \sin a \cos b}{a^2 + b^2} \right) dx^2 ,
\]</span> which differs from <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} df\)</span> by the terms coming from <span class="math inline">\(D\)</span>.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Autoparallels.</strong> In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span>, the autoparallel equation of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)</span> contains a single <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(j = 2\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(i = 1\)</span>: <span class="math display">\[
    \ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{V} = 0,
    \qquad
    \ddot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} + \frac{1}{\gamma^1_\mathcal{V}} \, \dot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{V} \, \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} = 0
    \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
    \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big( \gamma^1_\mathcal{V} \, \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} \Big) = 0 .
\]</span> Hence <span class="math inline">\(\gamma^1_\mathcal{V}(\lambda) = r_0 + u \lambda\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\gamma^1_\mathcal{V} \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} = w\)</span> constant, and the autoparallels are:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>for <span class="math inline">\(u = 0\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\gamma^2_\mathcal{V}(\lambda) = \varphi_0 + (w / r_0) \, \lambda\)</span>: <strong>circles</strong> traversed at constant speed. In particular <span class="math inline">\(\delta_{r_0}\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\delta}^i_\mathcal{V} = (0,1)\)</span>, is autoparallel for <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)</span>, while it was not for <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span>. At field level, <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{Y} = \partial y_2\left\lfloor \mathscr{Y}^1 \right\rceil e_2 = 0\)</span>, since the radial coordinate is constant along the circles;</p></li>
<li><p>for <span class="math inline">\(w = 0\)</span>, <strong>radial lines</strong>, <span class="math inline">\(\gamma^2_\mathcal{V} = \varphi_0\)</span>, the only curves that are autoparallel for both connections, in agreement with <span class="math inline">\(D^i_{j1} = 0\)</span>;</p></li>
<li><p>for <span class="math inline">\(u, w \neq 0\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\gamma^2_\mathcal{V}(\lambda) = \varphi_0 + \frac{w}{u} \ln\!\left( 1 + \frac{u \lambda}{r_0} \right)\)</span>, i.e. <span class="math inline">\(\gamma^1_\mathcal{V} = r_0 \, e^{u (\gamma^2_\mathcal{V} - \varphi_0) / w}\)</span>: <strong>logarithmic spirals</strong>.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>The vertical curves <span class="math inline">\(\gamma_{x_0}\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(x_0 \neq 0\)</span>, are no longer autoparallel: <span class="math inline">\(\ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{V} = x_0^2 / (x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^{3/2} \neq 0\)</span>. Note that the autoparallel equation only involves the symmetric part of the <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>’s: the torsion-free connection with the same symmetric part as <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)</span> has exactly the same autoparallels. Likewise, the normal coordinates of Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a> can remove the symmetric part <span class="math inline">\(\left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_y \right)^2_{(12)} = \frac{1}{2\beta_1}\)</span> at any given point, but no chart can remove the antisymmetric part <span class="math inline">\(\left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_y \right)^2_{[21]} = \frac{1}{2\beta_1}\)</span>, which is fixed by the torsion.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Parallel transport.</strong> By construction, <span class="math inline">\(e_1\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(e_2\)</span> are parallel along every curve, and a vector field is parallel along <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span> iff its frame components <span class="math inline">\(w^a\)</span> are constant along it. Along <span class="math inline">\(\delta_{r_0}\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\delta}^i_\mathcal{V} = (0,1)\)</span> and all <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^k_{j2}\)</span> vanish, so the parallel transport equations reduce to <span class="math inline">\(\dot{z}^k = 0\)</span> in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}\)</span>: <strong>parallel transport along the circles keeps the polar components constant</strong>. In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> the transported vector, <span class="math inline">\(\big( z^1 \cos \lambda - r_0 z^2 \sin \lambda, \; z^1 \sin \lambda + r_0 z^2 \cos \lambda \big)\)</span>, co-rotates with the circle, in sharp contrast with <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span>. In particular <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y} = \partial y_2\)</span> is parallel along the circles, whereas <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}\)</span>, with polar components <span class="math inline">\((\sin \lambda, \cos \lambda / r_0)\)</span> along <span class="math inline">\(\delta_{r_0}\)</span>, is not.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">C.5.4</span> A curved, torsion-free connection: <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\kappa}\)</span>`{=html} {#subsection_Example_Connections_curved}

```{=html}
<p>Neither of the previous connections is curved. Fix a constant <span class="math inline">\(\kappa &gt; 0\)</span> and define <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\kappa}\)</span> on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span> by a single non-vanishing coefficient function in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span>, <span class="math display">\[
    \left( \Gamma^{\kappa}_x \right)^1_{22} = \kappa \, a,
    \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad
    \nabla^{\kappa}_{\partial x_2} \partial x_2 = \kappa \, a \, \partial x_1,
    \quad \nabla^{\kappa}_{\partial x_1} \partial x_1 = \nabla^{\kappa}_{\partial x_1} \partial x_2 = \nabla^{\kappa}_{\partial x_2} \partial x_1 = 0 .
\]</span></p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Torsion and curvature.</strong> The coefficients are trivially symmetric in their lower indices, so <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\kappa}\)</span> is torsion free. In the Riemann curvature, every quadratic term <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^i_{rk} \Gamma^r_{jm}\)</span> can only be non-zero for <span class="math inline">\(r = 1\)</span>, and then contains a vanishing factor <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^i_{1k}\)</span>; the only non-vanishing derivative is <span class="math inline">\(\partial x_1\left\lfloor \Gamma^1_{22} \right\rceil = \kappa\)</span>. Hence the only non-vanishing components are <span class="math display">\[
    \mathrm{Riem}^1_{212} = \partial x_1\left\lfloor \Gamma^1_{22} \right\rceil - \partial x_2\left\lfloor \Gamma^1_{21} \right\rceil = \kappa = -\mathrm{Riem}^1_{221},
\]</span> and the Ricci curvature, <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Ric}_{ab} = \mathrm{Riem}^m_{amb}\)</span>, has the single component <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Ric}_{22} = \mathrm{Riem}^1_{212} = \kappa\)</span>, i.e. <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Ric} = \kappa \, dx^2 \otimes dx^2\)</span>. Being a tensor field that does not vanish in one chart, the curvature cannot be made to vanish in any other: no choice of chart makes all the <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>’s of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^\kappa\)</span> vanish on an open set.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Autoparallels.</strong> The autoparallel equation in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> reads <span class="math display">\[
    \ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{U} + \kappa \, \gamma^1_\mathcal{U} \, \big( \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} \big)^2 = 0,
    \qquad
    \ddot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = 0 .
\]</span> The second equation gives <span class="math inline">\(\gamma^2_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = b_0 + v \lambda\)</span>, and the first then becomes the harmonic oscillator <span class="math inline">\(\ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{U} + \kappa v^2 \gamma^1_\mathcal{U} = 0\)</span>, so that <span class="math display">\[
    \gamma^1_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = A \cos\!\big( \sqrt{\kappa} \, v \lambda + \psi \big)
    \quad \longrightarrow \quad
    a = A \cos\!\big( \sqrt{\kappa} \, (b - b_0) + \psi \big) :
\]</span> <strong>the autoparallels of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^\kappa\)</span> are sinusoids</strong> in the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span>, all with the same wave number <span class="math inline">\(\sqrt{\kappa}\)</span>, independently of the speed <span class="math inline">\(v\)</span>. Among our curves, only <span class="math inline">\(\gamma_0\)</span> (<span class="math inline">\(A = 0\)</span>) is autoparallel; for <span class="math inline">\(x_0 \neq 0\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\gamma_{x_0}\)</span> has acceleration <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^\kappa_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{X} = \nabla^\kappa_{\partial x_2} \partial x_2 = \kappa \, x_0 \, \partial x_1\)</span> along it.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Parallel transport around a loop.</strong> In the chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}\)</span> the parallel transport equations along a curve with velocity components <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}\)</span> are <span class="math inline">\(\dot{z}^1 + \kappa \, \gamma^1_\mathcal{U} \, z^2 \, \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = 0\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\dot{z}^2 = 0\)</span>. Transport a vector with components <span class="math inline">\((z^1, z^2)\)</span> counterclockwise around the rectangle <span class="math inline">\([x_0, x_1] \times [b_0, b_0 + \Delta b]\)</span>:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>along the two horizontal sides <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = 0\)</span>, so nothing changes;</p></li>
<li><p>up the right side, <span class="math inline">\(a = x_1\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = 1\)</span>, so <span class="math inline">\(z^1\)</span> changes by <span class="math inline">\(-\kappa \, x_1 \, z^2 \, \Delta b\)</span>;</p></li>
<li><p>down the left side, <span class="math inline">\(a = x_0\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = -1\)</span>, so <span class="math inline">\(z^1\)</span> changes by <span class="math inline">\(+\kappa \, x_0 \, z^2 \, \Delta b\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>After the full loop, <span class="math display">\[
    \Delta z^1 = -\kappa \, z^2 \, (x_1 - x_0) \, \Delta b = -\mathrm{Riem}^1_{212} \, z^2 \times \text{(area enclosed)},
    \qquad \Delta z^2 = 0 :
\]</span> <strong>the vector does not return to itself</strong>, and the mismatch is proportional to the curvature component, to the transported vector and to the enclosed area. Repeating the computation for <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{E}}\)</span> or <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)</span> gives <span class="math inline">\(\Delta z = 0\)</span> for every loop, as expected for flat connections (for <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)</span>, loops must avoid the origin).</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>

```
